units.translation: swiftly they were all visible to see
boldness not to be consorted with
rushing into battle with courageous boldness
he accomplished it with youthful boldness
boldness of black ruin for the halls
bringing boldness from sacrifices to dying men
not having all the dear boldness of hope
for this man is no small shield of boldness for us
where do you assign boldness to me?
In M θράξαι. Buttmann corrected it, Gramm. 1 p. 212, and Cobet, Nov. Lect. p. 655.
I hesitate to disturb your mind
θρασύνομαι: to become bold or confident
for shameful-counselling wretched madness, first cause of woe, emboldens mortals
so as to be more bold
before the ship was emboldened in its anchorage
from this seed will be born a bold man, famous with the bow
a bold man, as a commander
Ares, both civil and bold against each other
let him follow with voice, first of all, what is not bold
whom you must leave with bold heart and cross the Maeotic strait
for it is not fitting for the weaker to speak boldly
we marvel at your tongue, how bold-speaking it is
with fragments of oars and wreckage they struck
breaks the yoke in the middle
they broke the whole oared fleet
in a dochmiac verse, of which the first four syllables have fallen out, which I conjectured to have been νεόκοτα.
whence M repeats θρεομένη μέλη after v. 116, deleted by Porson.
I cry out fearful great griefs
to see the whole, the sojourners of the house will fall again, wailing

on which passage Eustath. p. 165: λέγονται δὲ τὸν μὲν ἄλλον πάντα χρόνον κομᾶν οἱ Ἕλληνες, ἐν δὲ πένθο πένθους καιρῷ κείρεσθαι · τηνικαῦτα γὰρ πλόκαμον κείραντες ἀνετίθουν Ἀπόλλωνι κουροτρόφῳ καὶ ποταμοῖς. καὶ ἦν οὗτος μὲν ὁ πλόκαμος θρεπτήριος κατὰ τὸν Αἰσχύλον, πενθητήριος δὲ ὁ ἕτερος. λέγεται δὲ τῆς τομῆς τοῦ θρεπτηρίου πλοκάμου κατάρξαι Θησεύς. κειράμενος γάρ, φασὶ, τὴν ἐμπροσθίαν κόμην εἰς Δῆλον ἀνέθετο τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι. [It is said that the Greeks wore their hair long at all other times, but in time of mourning they cut it; for then, having cut a lock, they dedicated it to Apollo the nourisher of youths and to the rivers. And this lock was the nourishing one according to Aeschylus, while the other was the mourning one. It is said that Theseus began the cutting of the nourishing lock; for having cut his front hair, they say, he dedicated it to Apollo in Delos.] More briefly the same at p. 1194 end, and the scholiast on Pindar Pyth. 4, 145, to whom we owe the preservation of these two verses.
